1041.explanation: Closing a hymn about how the world despises the penniless, Bhagat Kabir turns the question around: the truly poor person is the one whose heart lacks the Lord's Name. Gurbani thus admits the pain of material want while locating the deepest poverty elsewhere.
1041.tie_back: The Kural says nothing is more painful than poverty except poverty itself; Kabir agrees that poverty is the great affliction but redefines the worst poverty as spiritual emptiness.
1041.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1041._accuracy_note: Next-best: Kabir shares the Kural's sense that poverty is the gravest want, but he reframes it spiritually, which the Kural does not; only the opening half-line is quoted verbatim, the rest is paraphrase.

1042.quote_or_event: “I am so hungry, I cannot perform devotional worship service. Here, Lord, take back Your mala.”
1042.explanation: Bhagat Kabir tells God bluntly that a starving man cannot pray, and goes on to ask only for simple flour, ghee, lentils and bedding so that he can worship with love. Gurbani here recognises that grinding want blocks both worldly life and spiritual life.
1042.tie_back: The Kural says poverty robs a person of the joys of this life and the good of the next; Kabir confesses that hunger has made even his devotion, his path to the next world, impossible.
1042.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 656, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1042._accuracy_note: Strong fit: hunger destroying both bodily well-being and spiritual practice mirrors the Kural's loss of this world and the next, though Kabir's tone is a plea to God rather than a lament.

1043.quote_or_event: “The fire of desire is deep within; unsatisfied, people remain hungry and thirsty.”
1043.explanation: Guru Angad describes trishna (craving) as an inner fire that leaves people perpetually hungry and thirsty however much they have.
1043.tie_back: The Kural speaks of the hungry craving called poverty that destroys a family's ancient standing and good name; Guru Angad likewise names an insatiable inner hunger as the fire that consumes a person.
1043.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 138, Raag Majh, Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1043._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared word is craving, but Guru Angad means spiritual desire that afflicts rich and poor alike, and says nothing about loss of lineage or reputation.

1044.quote_or_event: “The hungry person does not care about honor, dishonor or harsh words.”
1044.explanation: In Gauri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan observes that someone driven by hunger stops weighing honour and shame and will put up with insults or speak without restraint to get food; he uses this as a simile for the seeker's single-minded longing.
1044.tie_back: The Kural says poverty breeds, even in the well-born, a weariness from which mean and shameful words come; Guru Arjan likewise notes that hunger erases a person's sense of honour and dishonour.
1044.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 317, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1044._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on want overriding one's sense of honour; the verse is used as a simile and does not mention good birth.

1045.quote_or_event: “So many endure distress, deprivation and constant abuse. Even these are Your Gifts, O Great Giver!”
1045.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak acknowledges that countless people live with suffering, hunger and continual blows, yet asks that even this be accepted as falling within God's hukam (divine order).
1045.tie_back: The Kural says every kind of sorrow gathers and settles within the single affliction of poverty; Guru Nanak names distress, hunger and abuse together as the lot of many, though he teaches acceptance rather than lament.
1045.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (Pauri 25), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1045._accuracy_note: Next-best: shares the picture of hunger bundled with many other sufferings, but Guru Nanak's point is surrender to hukam, a different emphasis from the Kural's lament.

1046.quote_or_event: “No one respects the poor man. He may make thousands of efforts, but no one pays any attention to him.”
1046.explanation: Bhagat Kabir describes with sharp realism how society ignores the destitute, however hard they try to be heard.
1046.tie_back: The Kural says that even when the poor speak sound truths, their words are disregarded; Kabir likewise says that whatever the poor man does, no one pays him any attention.
1046.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1046._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the poor being disregarded; Kabir speaks of efforts in general rather than specifically of wise speech.

1047.quote_or_event: “When the poor man goes to the rich man, and sits right in front of him, the rich man turns his back on him.”
1047.explanation: In the same hymn, Kabir pictures the poor man sitting face to face with a wealthy acquaintance who simply turns away, treating him as a stranger.
1047.tie_back: The Kural says one sunk in poverty is looked upon as a stranger even by his own mother; Kabir shows the same estrangement, as the rich man turns his back on the poor man in front of him.
1047.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1047._accuracy_note: Good fit on poverty making a person a stranger, but Kabir speaks of a rich man rather than one's own mother, and lacks the Kural's qualifier about poverty not joined to virtue.

1048.quote_or_event: “Why, O mind, do you plot and plan, when the Dear Lord Himself provides for your care?”
1048.explanation: In the evening prayer So Dar (Rehras), Guru Arjan rebukes the anxious mind that keeps scheming about tomorrow's livelihood, reminding it that God has already taken on its care. Sikh commentators stress that this forbids worry, not honest effort.
1048.tie_back: The Kural gives voice to the poor man's dread that yesterday's near-fatal want will return today; Guru Arjan addresses exactly that fearful planning and answers it with trust in God's provision.
1048.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1048._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse speaks to the same anxiety about livelihood but answers it rather than portraying it, so the parallel is one of response rather than shared sentiment.

1049.quote_or_event: “Fareed, I thought that I was in trouble; the whole world is in trouble! When I climbed the hill and looked around, I saw this fire in each and every home.”
1049.explanation: Sheikh Farid describes suffering as a fire that he first thought burned only in his own house, until a wider view showed it burning in every home.
1049.tie_back: The Kural says a man might sleep in the middle of fire but never in the middle of want; Farid likewise pictures human distress as a fire burning inside each household.
1049.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 81) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1049._accuracy_note: Next-best: the shared image is affliction as fire, but Farid speaks of universal suffering, not specifically of poverty or sleeplessness.

1050.quote_or_event: “But better than these is dry bread, if one sings the Glorious Praises of the Lord in the Society of the Saints.”
1050.explanation: Bhagat Kabir says that alms-bread eaten while praising God in holy company is better than royal wealth and pleasures. The Sikh Gurus, however, reject living by begging and ask even renunciants to earn by honest work.
1050.tie_back: The Kural says the utterly destitute should renounce fully rather than live off other people's salt and gruel; Kabir likewise prefers a bare, devotional life to grasping, but Sikh teaching as a whole rejects the renunciant path the Kural recommends.
1050.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 150) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1050._accuracy_note: Weak, next-best only: Kabir's preference for simple alms-bread with devotion touches the Kural's advice to renounce, but Sikh teaching rejects renunciation and begging, so the Kural's counsel conflicts with the Sikh householder ideal.
